verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, Go in to Pharaoh, and tell him, “This is what Yahweh says, ‘Let my people go, that they may serve me.
If you refuse to let them go, behold, I will plague all your borders with frogs:

and the river shall swarm with frogs, which shall go up and come into your house, and into your bedroom, and on your bed, and into the house of your servants, and on your people, and into your ovens, and into your kneading troughs:
and the frogs shall come up both on you, and on your people, and on all your servants.’”
Yahweh said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Stretch out your hand with your rod over the rivers, over the streams, and over the pools, and cause frogs to come up on the land of Egypt.’”
Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt; and the frogs came up, and covered the land of Egypt.
The magicians did the same thing with their enchantments, and brought up frogs on the land of Egypt.
Then Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron, and said, “Entreat Yahweh, that he take away the frogs from me, and from my people; and I will let the people go, that they may sacrifice to Yahweh.”

Moses said to Pharaoh, “I give you the honor of setting the time that I should pray for you, and for your servants, and for your people, that the frogs be destroyed from you and your houses, and remain in the river only.”
He said, “Tomorrow.” He said, “Be it according to your word, that you may know that there is no one like Yahweh our God.
The frogs shall depart from you, and from your houses, and from your servants, and from your people. They shall remain in the river only.”
Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh, and Moses cried to Yahweh concerning the frogs which he had brought on Pharaoh.
Yahweh did according to the word of Moses, and the frogs died out of the houses, out of the courts, and out of the fields.
They gathered them together in heaps, and the land stank.
But when Pharaoh saw that there was a respite, he hardened his heart, and didn’t listen to them, as Yahweh had spoken.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Stretch out your rod, and strike the dust of the earth, that it may become lice throughout all the land of Egypt.’”

They did so; and Aaron stretched out his hand with his rod, and struck the dust of the earth, and there were lice on man, and on animal; all the dust of the earth became lice throughout all the land of Egypt.
The magicians tried with their enchantments to produce lice, but they couldn’t. There were lice on man, and on animal.
Then the magicians said to Pharaoh, “This is God’s finger:” and Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he didn’t listen to them; as Yahweh had spoken.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Rise up early in the morning, and stand before Pharaoh; behold, he comes out to the water; and tell him, ‘This is what Yahweh says, “Let my people go, that they may serve me.

Else, if you will not let my people go, behold, I will send swarms of flies on you, and on your servants, and on your people, and into your houses: and the houses of the Egyptians shall be full of swarms of flies, and also the ground whereon they are.
I will set apart in that day the land of Goshen, in which my people dwell, that no swarms of flies shall be there; to the end you may know that I am Yahweh on the earth.
I will put a division between my people and your people: by tomorrow shall this sign be.”’”
Yahweh did so; and there came grievous swarms of flies into the house of Pharaoh, and into his servants’ houses: and in all the land of Egypt the land was corrupted by reason of the swarms of flies.
Pharaoh called for Moses and for Aaron, and said, “Go, sacrifice to your God in the land!”

Moses said, “It isn’t appropriate to do so; for we shall sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians to Yahweh our God. Behold, shall we sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians before their eyes, and won’t they stone us?
We will go three days’ journey into the wilderness, and sacrifice to Yahweh our God, as he shall command us.”
Pharaoh said, “I will let you go, that you may sacrifice to Yahweh your God in the wilderness, only you shall not go very far away. Pray for me.”

Moses said, “Behold, I go out from you, and I will pray to Yahweh that the swarms of flies may depart from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people, tomorrow; only don’t let Pharaoh deal deceitfully any more in not letting the people go to sacrifice to Yahweh.”
Moses went out from Pharaoh, and prayed to Yahweh.
Yahweh did according to the word of Moses, and he removed the swarms of flies from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people. There remained not one.
Pharaoh hardened his heart this time also, and he didn’t let the people go.

footnotes.content: Yahweh sends Moses in again to Pharaoh. Notice—He doesn't give up; He keeps speaking to a hardened heart, persistent as a grandfather who won't stop calling a wayward child home. Jesus does the same; He knocks, He calls, He waits for us to open the door.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The warning is clear: refusal brings consequence. Not out of cruelty, but because Pharaoh's resistance has a shape to it, and its name is plague. The Lord shows us the ledger before it's written—mercy always warns before it acts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The frogs will swarm everywhere—into your house, your bed, your oven where bread is made. In ancient Egypt, the Nile god Hapi was thought to bring fertility. Here, his domain becomes a plague. When we refuse the true God, even blessings curdle into chaos.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The frogs will be on you, on your people, on your servants—no one escapes. Hardness of heart doesn't protect; it spreads the suffering to everyone near. This is why we pray for leaders whose choices ripple outward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses speaks only—it's Aaron who stretches his hand with the rod. The rod is the sign of God's power, the same rod that parted the sea, that struck the rock. In Jesus, the rod becomes a shepherd's staff, still guiding us, still providing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aaron obeys, and the frogs rise and cover the land. No delay, no negotiation. When we align with God's will, things move—sometimes the thing we need to happen, sometimes the consequence we've earned. Either way, God's Word does not return empty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The magicians mimic the plague—they too can summon frogs. But notice: they can only copy what God does; they can't undo it, can't lead, can't save. False teachers always have just enough power to deceive, never enough to deliver.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Pharaoh breaks. He calls for Moses and Aaron, suddenly willing to negotiate. Suffering has a way of loosening our grip. He'll let them go—but notice his words: "Entreat Yahweh." He still thinks he's bargaining, not surrendering.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses honors Pharaoh by asking him to choose the time. "Set the hour when I should pray." It's a courtesy that won't soften the outcome, but it shows Moses's grace—he treats Pharaoh's pride with respect even as judgment falls. This is how the Lord often works with us too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh chooses tomorrow, and Moses agrees, adding a truth: "Be it according to your word, that you may know that there is no one like Yahweh our God." The purpose of the plague isn't just to free Israel; it's to teach Pharaoh who God really is.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The frogs will depart—a clean removal promised, not a negotiated mess. "They shall remain in the river only." God doesn't strike a deal where the frogs linger halfway; His mercies are complete, His judgments are full. When He releases, He releases.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses and Aaron leave Pharaoh and Moses cries to Yahweh. The Hebrew word suggests an urgent, fervent prayer—not casual, but earnest intercession. Here's a man who intercedes for his oppressor. Jesus teaches us to pray for those who persecute us; Moses lived it first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh does according to Moses's word, and the frogs die—not gradually, but decisively, out of houses and fields. God's mercy is as powerful as His judgment. When we ask in faith, the answer comes complete and clean.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They gather the dead frogs in heaps and the land stinks. This is the aftermath of hardness—not just the plague, but the stench, the mess, the cleanup. Sin always leaves a residue; grace removes the frogs, but the stink reminds us what happened.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Pharaoh sees relief, he hardens his heart again. He's had mercy, felt it, and turned away from it. This is the saddest verse in the plagues—not because of the judgment, but because Pharaoh refuses to learn. His heart becomes like stone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aaron strikes the dust and it becomes lice—tiny, relentless, invisible until they swarm. Lice were a profound indignity to Egyptians, who prided themselves on cleanliness. The next plague turns the very earth against them, attacking dignity itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aaron obeys, the dust becomes lice—and every speck of earth becomes an instrument of God's will. It's a reminder that creation itself belongs to the Creator and bends to His purpose. Nothing is outside His reach or His authority.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The magicians try to produce lice, but they can't. This is their limit—copying plagues is one thing, but creating life from dust? Only God can do that. False power always stumbles when it meets true creation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The magicians tell Pharaoh, "This is God's finger." They recognize divine action when they see it—even they know the difference between their tricks and His work. Yet Pharaoh still won't listen. He ignores the testimony of his own advisors.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh tells Moses to rise early and meet Pharaoh at the water. The water—where Egypt's god Hapi dwells. Moses confronts Pharaoh not in a chamber, but at the very seat of Egyptian power. The Lord meets us where our idols are.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The next plague: swarms of flies that will cover everything—houses, servants, people. Again, the warning comes first. The Lord always announces His judgment before He executes it; He never acts in secret with us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But the land of Goshen, where Israel dwells, will be spared—no swarms there. Even as judgment falls on Egypt, God separates His people. He doesn't exempt them from witnessing His power, but He protects them from His wrath. This is what the cross does for us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A division will be placed between God's people and Pharaoh's—by tomorrow, a sign. The Lord makes boundaries clear. His people are marked, set apart, known. There's no confusion about who belongs to Him and who doesn't.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The plague comes—grievous swarms that corrupt the land. Notice that Goshen is not even mentioned; it remains untouched. The separation is absolute. God's word is double-edged: judgment on those who refuse, mercy on those who trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh breaks again, calling for Moses and Aaron. "Go, sacrifice to your God in the land!" He's willing to compromise now—let them worship, but not leave. Compromise is how we think we can keep control; the Lord always calls for full surrender.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses explains: they must sacrifice to Yahweh what Egyptians call an abomination—likely referring to livestock Egyptians wouldn't eat or allow near their gods. To worship truly, Israel must leave Egypt; they cannot serve Yahweh on Pharaoh's soil.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three days' journey into the wilderness—a clean break, not a compromise. They need distance from Egypt's ways, its gods, its claims on them. Sometimes the Lord calls us to leave everything behind so we can worship freely. The wilderness is lonely, but it's pure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh agrees to let them go, but adds a condition: "only you shall not go very far away." He still thinks he's holding the leash. And he asks Moses to pray for him. Even now, he doesn't grasp that God's mercy is not negotiable; it's sovereign.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses promises to pray, but warns: "don't let Pharaoh deal deceitfully any more in not letting the people go." Moses knows Pharaoh's heart. He's seen the pattern—relief, hardening, refusal. He prays for the flies to leave but holds Pharaoh to account.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses went out from Pharaoh and prayed to Yahweh. Simple, brief, but profound—a man of God interceding for his enemy. The prayer itself is not recorded; only the act. Sometimes faithful prayer needs no words, only a willing heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh removes the flies—all of them, not one remains. Complete deliverance, as promised. God doesn't do half-measures. When He releases, it's total; when He restores, it's whole. This is the character of His mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh hardens his heart again—and we read it now and wonder how a man could be so blind. But readers today hear an echo in our own choices: the relief we feel, the promise we make, then the old grip tightening again. The Lord is patient, but He's not mocked. Once we start, repentance becomes harder each time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
